title: The Aftermath of the reservoir
premise: Ulyana Nystrom, a translator who has spent thirty years erasing the village dialect of his childhood, learns that his family's drowned homestead—submerged when a reservoir was built in 1989—is being auctioned as lakeside property now that the dam is being decommissioned. Returning to sell it quietly, he finds the water receding to expose not just foundations but evidence that his father's death during the flooding was no accident, and that the neighbors who stayed remember a different story than the one Ulyana was told. As he relearns the language he abandoned, he must choose between the legal settlement offered by the old power company and an unofficial reckoning demanded by the villagers, who want the truth spoken aloud in the tongue everyone pretends is dead. He ends by refusing both: he translates his father's last letter into the dying dialect and reads it at the exposed gravesite, letting the auction fail and the land return to common memory rather than private sale.
about_author: Y. M. Eriksen grew up between two languages on a fjord that was dammed for hydroelectric power, an experience they describe as 'learning to grieve in someone else's grammar.' They live in Trondheim, where they work as a court interpreter and write novels about what justice looks like when it arrives too late for the law.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, Oslo present day. A flawless translation job collapses when a client's word choice triggers a memory in a language he claims not to speak; that evening a solicitor's letter announces the auction of the Nystrom parcel beneath Lake Vessund. The beat is quiet dread—the past arriving as paperwork.

chapters.title: Water Over Everything
chapters.summary: Ulyana travels north, narrating the bus ride through terrain he knows in two vocabularies. In the town, shopkeepers greet him in dialect and he answers in Norwegian, watching their faces close. His aunt Signe refuses to discuss the house but slips him his father's old key. Beat: shame disguised as politeness.

chapters.title: What the Dam Took
chapters.summary: Ulyana visits the reservoir at dusk and meets Halvard, a former dam worker now obsessed with the decommissioning schedule, who mentions offhandedly that 'the water gives back what it took.' First glimpse of exposed stone walls. Beat: vertigo of recognition—he remembers swimming over this roof.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Ulyana attends the pre-auction viewing among developers and summer-home buyers, hearing his childhood described as 'prime waterfront.' An old neighbor, Brit, publicly names him as the drowned man's son and asks, in dialect, whether he has come to bury or to sell. Beat: exposure; invisibility fails.

chapters.title: Signe's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Signe finally speaks, giving her version of 1989: the company's rushed timeline, the night watchmen, the argument between Ulyana's father and the site manager. She insists the official drowning report was written by men who never came to the lake. Beat: grief sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Low Water
chapters.summary: Drought accelerates the drawdown; the homestead emerges fully. Ulyana wades out alone and finds inside the ruin a rusted toolbox containing his father's final unsent letter, water-damaged but legible in fragments. Beat: awe curdling into anger as the letter contradicts the accident narrative.

chapters.title: The Company Man
chapters.summary: A lawyer for the successor energy firm offers Ulyana a generous settlement with a confidentiality clause, revealing they know the letter exists. He recognizes the site manager's name from Signe's story—now a decorated retiree. Beat: temptation; the price of silence has never been higher.

chapters.title: Words Rising Like Fish
chapters.summary: Ulyana begins translating the damaged letter, and the dialect returns to him word by word, each recovered term unlocking a memory. The villagers gather informally in Brit's barn to hear fragments read aloud; Halvard brings the dam's original safety logs. Beat: belonging, hard-won and terrifying.

chapters.title: The Reading at the Waterline
chapters.summary: On auction morning, instead of attending, Ulyana stands on the exposed foundation and reads the full reconstructed letter aloud in dialect before the assembled village—and the company's observers. The letter names the negligence plainly. Bidders withdraw; the settlement offer dies in daylight. Beat: climax, truth as public act.

chapters.title: Common Ground
chapters.summary: Weeks later: the auction voided, the parish agrees to hold the land in trust as a memorial meadow. Ulyana stays through the first snow, teaching a few children the old words, and mails his resignation from the translation firm. Beat: resolution—belonging chosen, memory kept alive outside any courtroom.
